title: Equivalent and Comparing Fractions
seo_title: Grade 3 Equivalent and Comparing Fractions Worksheets (TEKS 3.3F, 3.3H, STAAR)
standard_text: 3.3F represent equivalent fractions with denominators of 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8 using a variety of objects and pictorial models, including number lines; 3.3G explain that two fractions are equivalent if and only if they are both represented by the same point on the number line or represent the same portion of a same size whole for an area model; 3.3H compare two fractions having the same numerator or denominator in problems by reasoning about their sizes and justifying the conclusion using symbols, words, objects, and pictorial models
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 worksheets for Texas TEKS 3.3F, 3.3G and 3.3H: equivalent fractions with strips and number lines, compare fractions with the same numerator or denominator, explain why, and word problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Equivalent fractions are at the same point on a number line.
key_sub: Same denominator: compare the numerators. Same numerator: fewer parts means bigger parts.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Equivalent fractions name the same amount: 12 = 24 = 48. On number lines, they are at the same point.
  • Same denominator: the parts are the same size, so compare the numerators. 58 > 38.
  • Same numerator: the fraction with fewer parts in the whole has bigger parts. 13 > 16.
  • Only compare fractions of the same-size whole.

Examples


1/2 and 2/4 are at the same point, so they are equivalent.

Example

Compare 2/3 and 2/6.

The numerators are the same: 2 parts each.

Thirds are bigger than sixths.

Answer: 2/3 > 2/6

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction: 1/8 > 1/4More parts in the whole means smaller parts.
Comparing halves of different-size wholesUse the same-size whole.
Thinking 2/4 = 2/8 because both have 2Fourths are bigger than eighths, so 2/4 > 2/8.

faq.a: Represent equivalent fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 using objects, pictures and number lines.

faq.q: How do you explain that two fractions are equivalent?
faq.a: Show that they are at the same point on number lines of the same length, or that they cover the same part of same-size wholes (TEKS 3.3G).

faq.q: How do you compare fractions with the same numerator?
faq.a: Look at the denominators. The fraction with the smaller denominator has bigger parts, so it is greater (TEKS 3.3H).

faq.q: Why must the wholes be the same size?
faq.a: Half of a large pizza is more than half of a small pizza. Fractions can only be compared when they refer to the same whole.
